turns.prompt_text: My mac mini is now located in Ames with me, however now my ssh-key for github no longer works
turns.response_html:
Since moving your Mac Mini means it underwent a hard reboot, the most likely culprit is either your SSH agent forgot the key when it powered down, or your new network environment is blocking standard SSH traffic.

Let's run a quick diagnostic to pinpoint exactly what's breaking, and look at how to fix it.

1. The Quick Diagnostic

Open your terminal on the Mac Mini and run the following command to see exactly how GitHub is rejecting the connection:

ssh -vT git@github.com

Look closely at the last few lines of the output:

  • If it says Permission denied (publickey), your Mac isn't offering the right key (or any key) to GitHub.
  • If it hangs indefinitely on Connecting to github.com... and times out, your new network is blocking port 22.

2. If it's "Permission Denied" (The Reboot Effect)

When macOS reboots, the temporary ssh-agent session clears out. If your key wasn't explicitly saved to your macOS Keychain, your terminal has no idea it exists.

First, check if your agent actually sees the key:

ssh-add -l

If it returns "The agent has no identities" or doesn't list your GitHub key, you just need to re-add it.

The Permanent Fix

To ensure you don’t have to deal with this every time the machine reboots, ensure your ~/.ssh/config file is telling macOS to pass the key to your keychain automatically.

  1. Open your SSH config file (e.g., nvim ~/.ssh/config or nano ~/.ssh/config).
  2. Make sure your GitHub block looks like this (replace id_ed25519 with your actual key name):
Host github.com
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  UseKeychain yes
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  1. Manually seed it into the keychain one last time:
ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

3. If it Times Out (The New Network Block)

If you're on a new local network, local ISP, or a strict Wi-Fi setup, outbound traffic on Port 22 might be restricted.

You can bypass this entirely by telling SSH to talk to GitHub over the HTTPS port (Port 443) instead, which is rarely blocked.

Open your ~/.ssh/config file and add or modify the GitHub host configuration to look like this:

Host github.com
  Hostname ssh.github.com
  Port 443
  User git
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  UseKeychain yes
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Test it again with ssh -T git@github.com to see if it punches through.

What did the ssh -vT debug output end up showing—a timeout or a publickey rejection?

turns.prompt_text: Ok, it just needed the keys added to the keychain, how can I automatically add them all at startup?
turns.response_html:
On macOS, you have two great ways to handle this. You can either let SSH lazy-load them automatically the first time you connect to a server, or you can force your shell to eagerly load all of them the second you open a terminal.

Method 1: The Global Lazy-Load (Recommended)

Instead of forcing a script to run on boot, you can configure SSH to automatically pull keys from your macOS Keychain on demand for every host you connect to.

Open your ~/.ssh/config file and add a wildcard block at the very top or bottom:

Host *
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  UseKeychain yes

Why this works perfectly:

The next time you restart your Mac Mini, the SSH agent will start completely empty. But the moment you run git fetch or ssh server, SSH sees Host *, automatically reaches into your macOS Keychain, pulls the correct passphrase, and loads the key into the agent for the rest of your session. You never have to manually run ssh-add again.

Method 2: Eager Load via Shell Startup

If you prefer to have your agent fully populated with all your keys the moment you launch a terminal session, you can add a trigger to your shell configuration.

Since macOS now uses --apple-load-keychain to re-seed the agent from the system keychain, you can add this to your ~/.config/fish/config.fish file:

# Re-seed the SSH agent with all keys stored in the macOS Keychain
if status is-interactive
    ssh-add --apple-load-keychain >/dev/null 2>&1
end

(If you are using Zsh instead of Fish for this specific machine's user account, you'd add ssh-add --apple-load-keychain >/dev/null 2>&1 to your ~/.zshrc instead).

⚠️ Note: For either method to work, make sure you've stored the key passphrases in the keychain at least once using the --apple-use-keychain flag: ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/your_key_name

Which approach fits better into your workflow—letting the system fetch them on demand, or loading the whole ring at terminal startup?
